clue.text: Centre-right is showing over-confidence

parts.note: a hub is the centre of a wheel or of activity
taken as written

explanation.surface: A politician of the centre-right is accused of arrogance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Centre-right' reads as one political term, but it splits into two pieces: the centre and the abbreviation for right.
explanation.definitionFit: Hubris is excessive pride or arrogant self-belief, the Greek tragic flaw, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Socialised with bosses it's said after husband died

parts.note: OB is obiit, Latin for died

indicators.note: the word for studded is heard, so its silent K drops away

parts.note: studded with bosses (round raised knobs) is knobbed

explanation.surface: A widow went out mixing with her superiors once her husband passed away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bosses' looks like managers, but bosses are raised studs, knobs.
explanation.definitionFit: To hobnob is to mix socially, especially with people of higher status, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Pair of spectacles in time for summer promotion

indicators.note: the pair goes inside the summer time abbreviation

parts.note: BST, British Summer Time, the UK's clock setting in summer
two round lenses look like OO

explanation.surface: Glasses go on sale in a summer marketing campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: BST is British Summer Time, when UK clocks go forward an hour.
explanation.definitionFit: A boost is a lift or promotion, as in giving sales a boost, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Reserve dough for cold sweet

parts.note: to put something on ice is to keep it in reserve, so ice means reserve
lolly is British slang for money, as is dough

explanation.surface: Keeping back some cash to buy a chilled treat.
explanation.walkthrough: LOLLY is British slang for money; 'dough' is money, not pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: An ice lolly is frozen flavoured water on a stick, a cold confection, so it is an example.

clue.text: In which The Red Baron might have come across Snoopy?

definitions.text: In which The Red Baron might have come across Snoopy?

parts.words: In which The Red Baron might have come across Snoopy?
parts.note: Snoopy the cartoon beagle fantasised about dogfights with the German air ace the Red Baron; read 'Snoopy' as nosy and the aircraft is one built for snooping, i.e. reconnaissance

explanation.surface: A cartoon question about the beagle's imaginary aerial duels with a German fighter pilot.
explanation.walkthrough: The Red Baron was Manfred von Richthofen, the First World War flying ace whom Snoopy battles in the Peanuts strip.
explanation.definitionFit: A reconnaissance aircraft is a snooping craft, so a snoopy plane is a pun on surveillance aircraft.

clue.text: Captain isn't so rattled in an emergency

indicators.note: rattled means shaken up, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, the apostrophe ignored
taken as written

explanation.surface: A ship's captain stays calm when things go wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Being at panic stations means being in a state of alarm or crisis, an idiom for emergency.

clue.text: One particular quadruped anteater can eat

indicators.note: the run of words can eat, that is swallow, a word within them

explanation.surface: A fussy four-legged insect-eater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One particular' reads as 'a certain one', but it means a fussy person.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedant is someone overly particular about small details, so 'particular' describes them.

clue.text: Letting oneself down in a bad way, concealing Daisy's illness

indicators.note: the unwell word hides the cow disease inside it

parts.note: ailing means unwell, in a bad way
Daisy is a typical name for a cow; BSE is bovine spongiform encephalopathy, mad cow disease

explanation.surface: A climber is in trouble, hiding a friend's sickness.
explanation.walkthrough: BSE, 'mad cow disease', hit British cattle in the 1990s; Daisy is a stock name for a cow.
explanation.definitionFit: Abseiling is descending a cliff by rope, literally letting oneself down, so the definition is witty.

clue.text: Course records flash up

parts.note: EPs are extended-play records

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the flash word is read backwards

parts.note: a mo, a moment, is a flash

explanation.surface: Lap times flash up on the screen at a racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: Epsom Downs, in Surrey, is the English racecourse where the Derby is run.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom is a famous racecourse, so it is an example of a course.

clue.text: Lassie, say, collecting zero and later poor grade in science

indicators.note: the dog's name takes in the next letter, so the zero is collected inside it
the poor grade is collected further along inside the same word, after the zero

parts.note: Lassie, the famous film collie, is a female dog, i.e. a bitch
E is a low exam grade
O looks like the figure zero

explanation.surface: A famous collie picks up a nought and then a failing mark in a science lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lassie, say' looks like a TV collie's name but stands for any female dog; 'collecting' and 'later' place the zero and then the low grade at two separate points inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Biotech, short for biotechnology, is a branch of applied science, so this is a straightforward example.

clue.text: It's fit for shelling rather than invasion by soldiers

definitions.text: It's fit for shelling rather than invasion by soldiers

parts.words: It's fit for shelling rather than invasion by soldiers
parts.note: military language disguises breakfast: soldiers are strips of toast dipped into a soft egg, while a firm-cooked one is peeled of its shell instead

explanation.surface: A position suited to bombardment rather than a ground assault.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'soldiers' are thin strips of toast for dipping into a soft-boiled egg.
explanation.definitionFit: A firmly cooked egg is peeled, not dipped into, so it suits shelling rather than soldiers.

clue.text: In reportedly fresh ways, detective exposed people

indicators.note: the detective is placed in the middle of the sound-alike and the streets
the word for fresh is heard rather than spelt, giving a spelling that matches its sound

parts.note: fresh means new
STS is short for streets, and streets are ways
DI is a Detective Inspector

explanation.surface: A detective, by all accounts using novel methods, unmasked the culprits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reportedly' gives the spelling NU, which sounds like 'new'; 'exposed' looks like 'unmasked' but means naked.
explanation.definitionFit: Nudists go about naked, so they are people who are exposed, quite literally.

clue.text: Better blooming swindle!

parts.note: flowers that are blooming are out
a do is a con or swindle, as in 'it was a do'

explanation.surface: An exclamation praising a better, flourishing con.
explanation.definitionFit: To better someone is to surpass or outdo them, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Check over sports field paid for by company

parts.note: a rec is a recreation ground, a public sports field in Britain
'on' means paid for, as in 'the drinks are on me'
a firm is a business company

explanation.surface: Inspecting a playing field that a business has sponsored.
explanation.walkthrough: A REC is the British short name for a recreation ground; 'by' simply links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To check something over again is to verify it a second time, which is what this verb means.

clue.text: Dome on University's left agent foaming

parts.note: a bubble is a domed covering or structure
Bath is a British university, so the possessive names the University of Bath

explanation.surface: A domed building stands to the left of a campus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on University's left' places the dome to the left of BATH, the University of Bath in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A bath product added to water to make foam is an agent that foams, so the description fits.

clue.text: Aid for stripper tossing both cowl and garter finally

indicators.note: tossing the words about mixes their letters

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of the word garter

explanation.surface: A burlesque dancer flings away a hood and stocking band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stripper' suggests a burlesque performer but is someone stripping paint.
explanation.definitionFit: A blowtorch is used to soften old paint for scraping, a tool for a paint stripper.

clue.text: Caribbean's quiet strand

parts.note: WI is the West Indies, the Caribbean islands, with the possessive S
P (piano) means quiet in music

explanation.surface: A thin strand of something from the quiet Caribbean.
explanation.definitionFit: A wisp is a thin strand, as of hair or smoke, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Meat skewered by long, fine implement

indicators.note: the meat has the other pieces driven through it

parts.note: pork is a meat
to long for is to itch for
F is short for fine, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Meat stuck on a long, slender kitchen tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A pitchfork is a farm tool for lifting hay, so it is an example of an implement.

clue.text: A cutting address to old cricketer making competitive drive

indicators.note: the letter cuts into the doctor's title and name

parts.note: W.G. Grace, the Victorian cricketer, was a doctor, so he was addressed as Dr Grace

explanation.surface: A sharp speech to a veteran batsman shows ambition.
explanation.walkthrough: W.G. Grace was England's great Victorian cricketer and a qualified doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: A drag race is a short acceleration contest between cars, a competitive drive.

clue.text: Christian healer fed one nothing

indicators.note: the healer has the other letters fed into the middle

parts.note: Dr, doctor, is a healer
I is the Roman numeral for one
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A Christian healer gives food to someone who has nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Christian' looks like a believer but is the first name of the couturier.
explanation.definitionFit: Christian Dior was the French fashion designer, so the first name is a fair indication of the surname.

clue.text: Entitlement that comes with Labour's last Act?

definitions.meaning: something you are entitled to by status or origin

definitions.text: that comes with Labour's last Act?
definitions.meaning: labour is childbirth, whose final act is the birth, so the second half is the actual birth itself as a right

explanation.surface: Wondering whether some privilege arrives with a political party's final piece of legislation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' with its capital looks like the British political party; it is the labour of giving birth.
explanation.definitionFit: A birthright is an entitlement you hold from birth, and labour ends in a birth, hence the pun.

clue.text: A frog I cooked that's devoured in Paris

indicators.note: cooked means doctored or rearranged, as with books

explanation.surface: Frogs' legs are cooked and eaten in a French restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devoured' means read avidly: Le Figaro is a Paris daily newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Le Figaro is a French daily paper, so it is something eagerly read in Paris.

clue.text: Light axe used in battle

indicators.note: the sacking word is placed inside the word for a fight

parts.note: a set-to is a fight or battle
to axe someone is to fire or sack them

explanation.surface: A lightweight axe was wielded in battle.
explanation.definitionFit: To light something is to ignite it, i.e. put a flame to it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Fawning son's address to Queen

definitions.note: the clue word is an adjective describing behaviour; the answer is the noun for such behaviour

parts.note: the Queen is addressed as ma'am, also spelt marm

explanation.surface: A son flatters by speaking to the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Smarm is ingratiating, oily flattery, so it names fawning behaviour.

clue.text: No good turning over what's burnt in grate

indicators.note: the two abbreviations are taken backwards

parts.note: N is short for number, written no.
ash is what remains after burning

explanation.surface: It's no use turning over the ashes in a fireplace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grate' looks like a fireplace with ash in it, but it is the verb, grinding teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: To grind or grate one's teeth together is a verb sense matching the definition here.

clue.text: Sue describing the cooker

definitions.meaning: to sue is to petition or ... for something, as in suing for peace
a cooker is a cooking fruit; an adjective describing such a fruit

explanation.surface: Taking legal action over a kitchen appliance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooker' looks like a stove, but in Britain it is also a cooking apple; a word describing one would be like an apple.
explanation.definitionFit: To sue for something is to make a formal request, so the verb is a synonym; the second is a jokey adjective.

clue.text: Fine time to arrest bishop for high aggression

indicators.note: the two outer pieces hold the bishop between them

parts.note: A1 means first-rate or fine, with the 1 read as I
an age is a period of time
RR is Right Reverend, the title of a bishop

explanation.surface: A good moment to arrest a bishop for violent behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Air rage is violent behaviour by a passenger on a plane, aggression high in the sky.

clue.text: Drive away carrying a policeman's washing

indicators.note: the shooing word carries the other letters inside it

parts.note: shoo is to drive away an animal
MP is a military policeman

explanation.surface: A policeman's laundry is being transported in a vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 's' stands for 'is'; 'Drive away' is a verb, not a car.
explanation.definitionFit: A shampoo is a wash of the hair, so washing is a fair noun synonym.

clue.text: John playing in periodical good game

indicators.note: the rearranged name is put inside the magazine

parts.note: a mag is a magazine, a periodical

indicators.note: John is playing about, i.e. its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man named John appears in a magazine article about a good game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'periodical' suggests a journal; the game is the Chinese tile game, here spelt with a double G at the end, which is why a separate 'good' is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Mah-jongg is a Chinese tile game for four players, so it is an example of a game.

clue.text: Chap using platform to cross railway

indicators.note: the platform spans the railway, holding it within

parts.note: a deck is a platform, as on a ship

explanation.surface: A man uses a footbridge to cross the railway line.
explanation.definitionFit: Deryck is a man's first name, and a chap is a man, so the name is an example.
